title: The coiled one remains
hookLine: what if four children were killed; the coiled serpent still lives, he writes (Zafarnama)

cards: Some sentences are short because nothing more could be said. The Zafarnama has one of those. Sikh tradition remembers what came before the letter: the Guru's four sons were killed.
Two, tradition says, fell fighting. Two, still small boys, were put to death because they would not give up their faith. You heard their story on days eighty-nine and ninety.
A father who had lost all four children wrote to the emperor, and the line he wrote about it is not a lament. It's a question, followed by an image Sikhs still repeat.

teach.h: WHAT OF IT, IF YOU KILLED FOUR CHILDREN?
teach.b: Paraphrased, the line runs like this: what of it, if you have killed four children? The coiled serpent still remains.
The first half names the worst thing that could happen to a parent, and names it flatly, almost as a shrug. That flatness is not coldness. It's refusal.
He will not let the loss be the end of the sentence. The second half turns to the coiled one.

teach.h: A COILED SERPENT: AT REST, ALIVE.
teach.b: A coiled snake is a snake at rest and fully alive, gathered into itself, not beaten. Readers hear different things in it.

teach.h: THE GURU, THE KHALSA, OR BOTH?
teach.b: Some hear the Guru speaking of himself: you took my sons, and I am still here. Some hear the Khalsa, the community he had formed: you can kill children, and you have not killed the people.

Some hear both, and a warning folded inside: a coiled thing can still rise. Whichever reading, the line is about what remains after the loss, not about the loss itself. And stay with what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say the grief is small. Sikhs remember the four sons, the Sahibzade, with deep sorrow, in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their deaths.
The coiled one remains is not a way of skipping the mourning.
It's what stands up in the middle of it.

how: Sikhs remember the four Sahibzade in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their martyrdom; the Zafarnama's line about the coiled serpent is often recited in katha and at those gatherings.

games.q: what does “the coiled one remains” mean?
o: what wasn't defeated still lives on after the loss
a snake that guarded the Guru's door at night
a curse laid on the emperor and all his heirs

games.q: the line and its readings: tap the pairs.
p: names the loss of four children
the Guru himself is still here
the Khalsa has not been killed

s: the line says the grief over his sons is small
it refuses to let the loss end the sentence; Sikhs remember the Sahibzade with deep sorrow.
readers hear more than one meaning in the coiled serpent
the Guru, the Khalsa, or both, with a warning folded inside.
a coiled snake in the image is a beaten snake
coiled means gathered and alive, at rest, not defeated.

games.q: you've lost all four of your children, and you're writing to the man whose rule took them. what does your sentence about them do?
o: dwell on the grief for pages.
name the loss flatly, then say what remains.
games.why: the Guru names it in a single question, what of it, if you killed four children? then turns at once: the coiled serpent still remains.

practice: If it feels right, bring to mind a loss you've carried and let it be as heavy as it is; then, gently, look for what is still standing in you: a habit you kept, someone you still look after, a way you still laugh.
If you pray, hold both the loss and what remains in Waheguru. If a loss ever feels heavier than you can carry, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: The coiled one remains. In the Zafarnama, after naming the killing of his four sons, Guru Gobind Singh writes that the coiled serpent still lives. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: still standing. Coiled and quiet is not the same as beaten. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Zafarnama (Dasam Granth), the verse on the four children and the coiled serpent
